messages.subject: NaNs and Ragged Arrays
parts:
I have data which is related to a series of events (keystrokes) on a collection of individuals.  It is a ragged array as each individual has a different number of events.

This is not too difficult to model as I simply put it in an array with rows representing individuals and columns representing events and then fill the irrelevant parts with NAs.

The relevant parts of my model are:
Enter code here...data {

  /* Fixed Structural Parameters */
  int<lower=1> I;    //number of essays, index for essays
  int<lower=1> J[I]; // number of events per essay,  index for events,
  int<lower=1> Jmax;  //Jmax <- max(J);

  ...

  /* Data */
  matrix[I,Jmax] Y;               // log pause time
}
parameters {...}
model {
  ...
  /* Likelihood for data */
  for (i in 1:I) {
    for (j in 1:J[i]) {
      ... // Do things with Y[i,j]
    }
  }
}




It shouldn't matter what I fill the values of Y[i,j] for j>J[i] with as these values are never scanned.  In R, I fill them with NAs, so if I accidentally reference one of those cells I'll get an error message or NAs all over indicating that I accidentally accessed an illegal value.  I would like to do the same thing in Stan.  I can understand why you don't want to deal with the overhead of R's NA handling, but it seems to me that IEEE NaNs would be perfect for the job and would not require any modification to the code.  (Yes, they might produce run time errors, but that would be fine).

However, when I try to read the data into Stan, it complains about the NAs.  This is true if I change all of the NAs to NaNs in R.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NaNs and Ragged Arrays
parts:
We don't yet support reading in NaNs in CmdStan --- I'm not
sure what the status is on the R side, as that's where the
reading is done for R.

There's a suggestion for coding ragged arrays in the manual.
Subection "Representing Ragged Arrays in Stan" in the section
on "Naive Bayes Classification and Clustering" in the chapter
on "Clustering Models".

We should probably foreground this coding a bit more, maybe
moving it into the section on arrays and matrices. We're about
to majorly reorganize the manual in an attempt to make it easier
to read and index.

- Bob

parts:
I should have been more specific.  This is in RStan.  The model compiles
and then gives me a message about not accepting missing values.  I still
get the same message when I recode all of the NAs to NaNs.

I can work around the problem by just sticking in a highly unusual value
(I'm using 9999 when the units should be log(seconds)).  But this makes
it harder to check for illegal access to the missing values.

I think what I really want is a way to suppress the NA check when loading
data and just let Stan generate a runtime error (or return NaNs) if I accidentally
access the out of bounds data.  It would make me feel more secure.

  --Russell

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: RStan (and CmdStan and PyStan) NaN/inf in I/O
parts: [changed subject]

On May 5, 2014, at 5:14 PM, Russell Almond <alm...@acm.org> wrote:

> I should have been more specific. This is in RStan. The model compiles
> and then gives me a message about not accepting missing values. I still
> get the same message when I recode all of the NAs to NaNs.
>

Sorry to be confusing. Here's the issue I created for RStan:

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/67

and for Stan C++ (which will fix the problem in CmdStan):

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/637

There's actually nothing conceptually difficult about our accepting
all the valid IEEE floating-point values (finite values, NaN, +inf, -inf).

I didn't know what the Python status was, so I didn't create an issue.

> I can work around the problem by just sticking in a highly unusual value
> (I'm using 9999 when the units should be log(seconds)). But this makes
> it harder to check for illegal access to the missing values.

Right --- not a strategy we want to promote long term, but it's what
we've been doing ourselves in some cases. The problem is that NaN also
isn't a good distinguished code point.

It really will be better to just reformulate the data/parameters for
Stan if possible.

> I think what I really want is a way to suppress the NA check when loading
> data

I'm not sure what the NA check is, but if RStan looks for NA values and
gripes, that's the right behavior --- there's no way for us to get an
NA into Stan. We can deal with NaN and +/- inf, but not NA. And I don't
want to just convert NA to NaN, at least not by default.

> and just let Stan generate a runtime error (or return NaNs) if I accidentally
> access the out of bounds data. It would make me feel more secure.

Not sure what you mean here. You mean convert the NA to NaN? I'd rather
see users do that explicitly on the outside from R. R's the only platform
that has the special NA value. It's not something we plan to support inside
of Stan.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: NaNs and Ragged Arrays
parts:
Two thoughts:.

One, I tested in the R console and is.na(NaN) returns TRUE.  I'm pretty sure that the same thing is true for the C function isNA.  This explains why the behaviour was the same for NA and NaN.

The second thought is that you might want an "allowNaN" flag to allow accepting non-finite values.  That way you get around people simply putting in NAs for missing data and assuming that Stan will magically impute without any kind of imputation model.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: NaNs and Ragged Arrays
parts:
On May 6, 2014, at 12:40 AM, Russell Almond <alm...@acm.org> wrote:

> Two thoughts:.

Thanks for following up. You've started a discussion on the dev side
about whether we want to support something like NA and I think the
jury's going to be out for a while on this one, because those of us
coming from a C++/programming background have a rather different view
on the matter than those of us coming from an R/stats background.
(Not saying one is right or wrong, just that we don't all agree on
whether NA is worth the hassle or not.)

>
> One, I tested in the R console and is.na(NaN) returns TRUE.

I think this just shows how broken R's type system is!
is.nan(NA) is FALSE and is.nan(NaN) is TRUE, so why they decided
to treat NaN as a kind of NA is beyond me.
> I'm pretty sure that the same thing is true for the C function isNA. This explains why the behaviour was the same for NA and NaN.

What C(++) function are you talking about? There's no NA values
in C++, just IEEE arithmetic.
> The second thought is that you might want an "allowNaN" flag to allow accepting non-finite values.

I'm not sure what you're suggesting here in terms of values in
R and how they're rendered in Stan. Stan simply doesn't have an
NA value (Ben suggested following Stata and reserving the largest
double values for special uses, but I'm still skeptical).
> That way you get around people simply putting in NAs for missing data and assuming that Stan will magically impute without any kind of imputation model.

I don't think we're going to go to any kind of non-explicit imputation scheme.

- Bob

Bob,
I'd vote for NAs.

I think you might have things the wrong way around when you say

"I think this just shows how broken R's type system is!
is.nan(NA) is FALSE and is.nan(NaN) is TRUE, so why they decided
to treat NaN as a kind of NA is beyond me."

I could be mistaken, but it is my understanding that the original R authors chose a special value of an NaN as NA a long time ago so this is perfectly sensible.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: NaNs and Ragged Arrays
parts:
On May 6, 2014, at 12:19 PM, Sean O'Riordain <seor...@tcd.ie> wrote:

> Bob,
> I'd vote for NAs.
>

You're not alone!

Lots of people like R's way of doing things, too. But I find almost
every decision they made very confusing from a computer science perspective.
Python, on the other hand, does almost everything the way I would expect
a scripting language to behave.

> I think you might have things the wrong way around when you say
> "I think this just shows how broken R's type system is!
> is.nan(NA) is FALSE and is.nan(NaN) is TRUE, so why they decided
> to treat NaN as a kind of NA is beyond me."

Just to be perfectly clear, it's not the existence of NA that I
object to, but the *** line, which treats NaN as a kind of NA.

is.nan(NA) : FALSE
is.nan(NaN) : TRUE

is.na(NA) : TRUE
is.na(NaN) : TRUE ***

If you're going to have NA mean "undefined" and NaN mean ill-defined (i.e., 0/0
or 0 * infinity), you don't want to confuse them, no matter how they're represented
internally.

I find this kind of thing very very confusing:

> a = 0/0

> exists("a")
[1] TRUE

> is.na(a)
[1] TRUE

You get the same thing if you just set a = NA, which is why it doesn't
feel to me like it's truly an "undefined" value, because that's not how
it behaves semantically.
> I could be mistaken, but it is my understanding that the original R authors chose a special value of an NaN as NA a long time ago so this is perfectly sensible.

People definitely have different opinions on these things. As
you can see if you follow our recent stan-dev discussion. No idea
what we'll do about it long term.

- Bob
